chapter_title: Efficient Data Management with Storage Maps

screens.title: Efficient Data Management with Storage Maps
screens.subtitle: How StorageMap and StorageDoubleMap help you store and query on-chain relationships efficiently

narration.text: In this lesson we'll explore two storage primitives that become essential as your pallet grows: StorageMap and StorageDoubleMap. These are the on-chain key-value structures that let you associate data with identifiers—account IDs, asset IDs, or pairs of identifiers—so lookups are direct and cheap compared to iterating through large values. You'll learn the common declaration patterns, why the hasher choice matters, and how to interact with maps from dispatchable functions using safe arithmetic and checks. We'll ground the ideas with concrete examples: a Balances map for per-account balances and an Allowance double map for owner-spender approvals. I will also highlight common beginner mistakes, such as storing unbounded vectors in a map or misusing identity hasher, and show safer alternatives. By the end you will know when a single-key map is sufficient, when a two-key double map saves costly iteration, and how to design storage access to keep your pallet performant and economically viable. Consider how a direct lookup instead of scanning a list reduces both C P U and transaction fee costs—what on-chain relationship in your project could benefit from this pattern?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Use StorageMap for single-key lookups and StorageDoubleMap when relationships are naturally keyed by two identifiers; choose hashers and access patterns to minimize reads and writes.

Efficient Data Management with Storage Maps

Learn how on-chain key-value storage in Substrate reduces expensive lookups, and how to select StorageMap or StorageDoubleMap to model relationships cleanly and efficiently.

narration.text: These objectives map directly to practical skills you will use when building Substrate pallets. First, you will understand why StorageMap and StorageDoubleMap exist and when to choose each. That means recognizing access patterns: single-key lookups versus relationships keyed by two identifiers. Second, you will implement StorageMap declarations and use generated accessors to insert, retrieve, and remove entries safely. You will see how a balances map is declared and how to update it in a transfer flow. Third, you will implement StorageDoubleMap for multi-key access patterns and use it to represent approvals or paired relationships so queries remain direct and efficient. Finally, you will learn best practices: pick appropriate hashers, use checked arithmetic and existence checks, and avoid unbounded storage like raw vectors when possible. Each objective includes a small mnemonic or visual cue so you remember the distinction between single-key and two-key storage. By the end you will be able to design storage that balances simplicity, performance, and on-chain cost.

screens.title: What are StorageMap and StorageDoubleMap?
screens.subtitle: Definitions, core behavior, and mental model

narration.text: A StorageMap is a single-keyed on-chain key-value mapping. Think of it as a hash map stored in the runtime state where the key is an identifier such as an account ID and the value is the data you associate with that identifier. The generated getter gives you direct access by key, so reading a balance for a user is an O(1) lookup from the chain's perspective. A StorageDoubleMap extends that idea to two keys. It stores values indexed by a pair—commonly used for relationships like owner and spender in token approvals. The important claim is this: a double map lets you query a single owner-spender pair directly without iterating through all approvals, which on-chain would be prohibitively expensive. Concrete example: Balances as StorageMap maps AccountId to Balance; Allowance as StorageDoubleMap maps Owner and Spender to an approved amount. A common misconception is to treat double maps as nested maps in memory; while conceptually similar, Substrate stores them with composed keys and specific hashers so the lookups remain constant time. Takeaway: match your data access pattern to the map type—use single-key maps for one-dimensional lookups and double maps when two dimensions are the primary query.

keyIdea.title: Definition takeaway
keyIdea.text: StorageMap is for single-key lookups; StorageDoubleMap is for pair-keyed relationships—use them to avoid expensive iteration.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Definitions
Core Concept

StorageMap and StorageDoubleMap

StorageMap stores a single value per key. StorageDoubleMap stores a value per pair of keys. Both generate convenient accessors via the decl_storage macro and support insert, get, remove, and contains_key operations.

StorageMap example
Balances: AccountId => Balance for direct per-account lookup.
StorageDoubleMap example
Allowance: (Owner, Spender) => approved amount for direct owner-spender lookup.
Quick Notes
  • Use contains_key when only existence matters.
  • Prefer direct lookups over storing and scanning lists.
  • Understand that hashers affect storage layout and performance.
Key Takeaway

Match the map type to your primary lookup pattern to minimize chain work and fees.

screens.title: Declaring a Balances StorageMap
screens.subtitle: How to declare and use a StorageMap for per-account balances

narration.text: Let's walk through a canonical StorageMap declaration and how it's used. In the decl_storage macro you declare Balances as a map from AccountId to Balance. The macro generates a getter that you can call to read the value, and methods like insert and remove to update the state. A concrete pattern in a transfer function is: read the sender's balance with the generated getter, ensure it is sufficient using an ensure check, compute new balances via checked_sub and checked_add to avoid arithmetic errors, then insert the updated balances back into storage. An important example to highlight is using unwrap_or_default when a recipient has no existing balance; this sets their balance to zero before adding. A common misconception is assuming get always returns a value; it returns an option-like default behavior based on declaration, so handle absences explicitly. Practically, using contains_key for existence-only checks avoids an unnecessary full get and potential unwrapping work. This pattern keeps reads and writes clear and minimizes unexpected panics or arithmetic overflows. Declaring a Balances StorageMap means read current value, validate, compute safely with checked arithmetic, and write back using insert.. In practical terms, how to declare and use a storagemap for per-account balances. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical pattern
keyIdea.text: Read current value, validate, compute safely with checked arithmetic, and write back using insert.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Balances Map
Code Walkthrough

Declare Balances and common access pattern

The declaration creates get and insert helpers. Use get to read, contains_key when you only need presence, and insert to write the updated value after safe arithmetic.

// Example Balances StorageMap (rust-like pseudocode)
decl_storage! {
    trait Store for Module<T: Config> as Balances {
        Balances get(fn balances): map hasher(blake2_128_concat) T::AccountId => T::Balance;
    }
}

// In a transfer dispatchable:
let sender_balance = Self::balances(&sender);
ensure!(sender_balance >= amount, Error::InsufficientBalance);
let to_balance = Self::balances(&to);
let new_sender = sender_balance.checked_sub(&amount).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?;
let new_to = to_balance.checked_add(&amount).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?;
Self::Balances::insert(&sender, new_sender);
Self::Balances::insert(&to, new_to);
Explanation
  • Use blake2_128_concat hasher for general keys for safety and range queries.
  • Prefer contains_key when you only need to know if an entry exists.
  • Use checked arithmetic to prevent overflow/underflow and ensure! to validate preconditions.
Key Takeaway

Always handle missing keys and arithmetic safely before writing to storage.

screens.title: Allowance as a StorageDoubleMap
screens.subtitle: Declare a double map for owner-spender approvals and use direct lookups

narration.text: A StorageDoubleMap is ideal when your data is naturally keyed by a pair. For token allowances, you want to check how much an owner has allowed a spender to use. A double map declaration specifies two key hashers and the value type. The macro generates typed accessors so you can get, insert, or remove an approval for a given owner and spender pair. Concrete usage looks like calling the generated get with a tuple of owner and spender or using insert with the pair to set a new allowance. This direct lookup avoids iterating through all approvals. A common mistake is trying to model two-key lookups with nested single-key maps; that adds unnecessary complexity or extra reads. Instead, a double map keeps the runtime storage layout efficient and the code clearer. Remember to remove approvals when ownership changes to avoid stale permissions. The efficiency gains are especially visible on-chain where every read costs resources; direct pair lookup reduces both C P U and storage costs compared with scanning lists. Allowance as a StorageDoubleMap means double maps provide direct, two-key lookups for relationships and avoid iteration over collections on-chain.. In practical terms, declare a double map for owner-spender approvals and use direct lookups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DoubleMap advantage
keyIdea.text: Double maps provide direct, two-key lookups for relationships and avoid iteration over collections on-chain.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Allowance DoubleMap
Code Walkthrough

Declare Allowance and common usage

A double map declaration takes two hashers and two key types, then the value. Use the generated helpers with a pair of keys when reading or writing.

// Example Allowance StorageDoubleMap (rust-like pseudocode)
decl_storage! {
    trait Store for Module<T: Config> as Assets {
        Allowance get(fn allowance): double_map
            hasher(blake2_128_concat) T::AccountId,
            hasher(blake2_128_concat) T::AccountId
            => T::Balance;
    }
}

// Access examples:
let amount = Self::Allowance::get((&owner, &spender));
Self::Allowance::insert((&owner, &spender), new_amount);
Self::Allowance::remove((&owner, &spender));
Why it matters
  • Directly query an owner-spender pair without scanning all approvals.
  • Remove approvals when state changes to avoid leaked permissions.
  • Prefer double map over nested maps for cleaner runtime access and fewer reads.
Key Takeaway

Model dual-key relationships with StorageDoubleMap to keep lookups constant time and code simple.

screens.title: Interacting with maps in dispatchable functions
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step transfer flow using StorageMap

narration.text: When you interact with storage maps in dispatchables you should follow a small, repeatable process. First, validate the caller with ensure to confirm a signed origin. Second, retrieve current values using the generated getter and handle missing entries explicitly—either with default values or pattern matching. Third, validate preconditions such as sufficient balance using ensure. Fourth, perform arithmetic with checked_add and checked_sub to prevent overflow or underflow and return a clear error if the operation fails. Fifth, update storage by calling insert for each modified key and remove entries when they become unnecessary. Sixth, emit events to record the state change. Concrete example: in a transfer you read sender balance, ensure it's enough, read recipient balance or default to zero, calculate new balances safely, insert new balances, and optionally remove zero balances to keep storage compact. A misconception to avoid is assuming reading a value is free; every storage access consumes resources, so minimize redundant reads and writes. The closing question: how can you structure your dispatchable functions to minimize the number of writes while preserving correctness? Interacting with maps in dispatchable functions means validate origin, read safely, check preconditions, use checked arithmetic, write updates, and emit events.. In practical terms, a step-by-step transfer flow using storagemap. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Interaction pattern
keyIdea.text: Validate origin, read safely, check preconditions, use checked arithmetic, write updates, and emit events.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Dispatchable Flow
Process Flow

Transfer: step-by-step

1. Validate origin
Use ensure_signed to get caller and fail early if not signed.
2. Read values and handle absence
Call generated getter. Use unwrap_or_default or match on Option to handle missing data.
3. Validate and compute safely
Use ensure to check sufficiency and checked_sub/checked_add for arithmetic.
4. Update storage and emit event
Insert new balances and emit a transfer event. Remove entries if they become unnecessary.
Example
// transfer pattern (pseudocode)
let sender = ensure_signed(origin)?;
let sender_bal = Self::balances(&sender);
ensure!(sender_bal >= amount, Error::InsufficientBalance);
let to_bal = Self::balances(&to);
let new_sender = sender_bal.checked_sub(&amount).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?;
let new_to = to_bal.checked_add(&amount).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?;
Self::Balances::insert(&sender, new_sender);
Self::Balances::insert(&to, new_to);
// emit event
Common Mistake

Reading then writing a large vector field frequently is expensive; prefer keyed storage or off-chain indexing for heavy aggregations.

screens.title: Approve and disapprove with StorageDoubleMap
screens.subtitle: Insert and remove owner-spender approvals safely

narration.text: Approving a spender and revoking that approval are straightforward when using a StorageDoubleMap. Approve inserts a value keyed by the owner and the spender. Disapprove removes that specific pair. The concrete sequence is: check the caller is the owner, insert the approval into the double map, and emit an Approval event. For disapproval, validate owner, call remove with the pair of keys, and emit a revocation event. A subtle but important detail is cleanup when ownership or token state changes: any approvals tied to that token should be removed to avoid lingering permissions. A misconception is to try and store approvals as a list under the owner and search for spender entries; that leads to expensive writes and potential concurrency issues. Using the double map gives direct insert and remove operations for a specific pair. When writing these functions, be mindful of gas: avoid unnecessary reads of large structures and prefer direct keyed access with insert and remove. Approve and disapprove with StorageDoubleMap means use insert and remove on a double map keyed by owner and spender. clean up approvals on ownership changes.. In practical terms, insert and remove owner-spender approvals safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Approval pattern
keyIdea.text: Use insert and remove on a double map keyed by owner and spender. Clean up approvals on ownership changes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Approve Flow
Process

approve and disapprove

Insert an approval for an owner-spender pair and remove it when needed. Validate ownership and keep operations minimal.

// approve (pseudocode)
let owner = ensure_signed(origin)?;
ensure!(owner == current_owner_of(nft), Error::NotNftOwner);
Self::NftApprovals::insert((&nft_id, &approved_spender), ());
// disapprove
Self::NftApprovals::remove((&nft_id, &disapproved_spender));
Notes
  • Use unit value when presence alone indicates approval.
  • Remove approvals on transfer to avoid stale permissions.
  • Avoid storing many approvals in a single vector under an owner.
Key Takeaway

Direct insert/remove on the double map keeps approvals efficient and auditable.

screens.title: Choosing a hasher: blake2_128_concat and alternatives
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs between common hasher choices and when to use identity

narration.text: Hashers determine how keys are turned into storage keys. The chapter recommends blake2_128_concat as a strong default: it hashes the key and appends the original, enabling efficient range queries while preserving uniqueness and good performance. Two alternatives are twox_64_concat, which is faster but less collision-resistant for certain workloads, and identity, which stores the key directly without hashing. Identity is only appropriate when keys are fixed-size and already unique; using identity with variable-length keys can harm efficiency and security. A practical example: when your key is an AccountId with fixed length, identity might be okay in a tightly controlled situation, but blake2_128_concat remains safer for general use. A common misconception is that hashing always slows things materially on modern chains. While hashing adds C P U cost, it improves storage layout and reduces collision risk, and the right choice balances security, range query needs, and performance. The closing check: for your pallet, ask whether you need fast range scans, absolute speed, or minimal storage risk to pick the appropriate hasher. Choosing a hasher: blake2_128_concat and alternatives means prefer blake2_128_concat as a general choice; use identity only for fixed-size, pre-validated keys.. In practical terms, trade-offs between common hasher choices and when to use identity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hasher selection
keyIdea.text: Prefer blake2_128_concat as a general choice; use identity only for fixed-size, pre-validated keys.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Hasher Choices
blake2_128_concat

Good default: hashes key and concatenates original, enables range queries and balanced performance/security.

twox_64_concat

Faster hashing, less collision resistance. Useful for high-throughput keys where collision risk is acceptable.

identity

Stores keys directly. Only for fixed-size, already-validated keys; otherwise avoid due to security and layout concerns.

Practical question

Do you need range queries or absolute minimal CPU cost? If range queries are important, prefer blake2_128_concat; if keys are fixed and throughput is the top priority, evaluate twox_64_concat or identity carefully.

screens.title: Why not store Vecs of IDs on-chain?
screens.subtitle: State bloat, update costs, and safer alternatives

narration.text: A common beginner proposal is to store a vector of IDs under a StorageMap keyed by account, for example mapping an AccountId to a Vec of NFT IDs. This seems convenient, but it creates several problems. First, vectors are unbounded: as the list grows, reading, modifying, and writing the entire vector becomes increasingly expensive and will raise transaction fees. Second, concurrent updates become complicated because two transactions trying to modify the same vector must coordinate or one will fail, leading to user friction. Third, queries that only need to check ownership of a single NFT become inefficient because you must read and scan the entire vector. The recommended alternatives are either to store ownership per NFT using StorageMap from NftId to AccountId, or if an on-chain list is required and bounded use a BoundedVec with a known maximum size. Off-chain indexing services are also a safer option for retrieving lists of items efficiently. Concrete example: to check if Alice owns NFT 42, a StorageMap from NftId to AccountId is a single-key direct lookup; storing a Vec forces you to read Alice's entire list and scan it. The takeaway: favor keyed lookups on-chain and push large aggregations off-chain when possible.

keyIdea.title: Design rule
keyIdea.text: Avoid unbounded Vec in storage; prefer per-item keyed maps or off-chain indexing for aggregations.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Vec Pitfalls

Why storing Vec<NftId> under AccountId is risky

  • Unbounded growth increases read/write cost and state size.
  • Concurrent updates can conflict, causing failed transactions.
  • Single-item checks require scanning the whole vector.
Common Mistake
Choosing convenience over scalability by storing ever-growing collections on-chain.

Better alternatives

  • Use StorageMap<NftId, AccountId> for direct ownership lookup.
  • If a bounded list is required on-chain, use BoundedVec with a strict cap.
  • Rely on off-chain indexing for large aggregations and lists.
Key Takeaway

Model per-item ownership with keyed maps and keep heavy aggregation off-chain.

screens.title: Handling Option, ensure!, and checked arithmetic
screens.subtitle: Prevent underflows, validate inputs, and handle missing entries

narration.text: Safety is non-negotiable in on-chain code. When a getter might return no value, treat that case explicitly. Use pattern matching or unwrap_or_default to provide a safe fallback where appropriate. For numeric updates, prefer checked_add and checked_sub, which return an option-like result that you can convert to an error with ok_or. Combine arithmetic checks with ensure macros to enforce preconditions such as sufficient balance or valid identifiers. For example, before subtracting an amount from a sender’s balance, ensure the balance is at least the transfer amount, then use checked_sub to compute the new balance; if checked_sub returns None, return a clear overflow error. Another frequent pattern is using contains_key when you only need to know presence rather than retrieving the full value; this reduces unnecessary reads. A misconception is assuming unwrap_or_default is always safe; if defaulting hides a missing invariant, it may mask bugs. The closing question: which operations in your pallet require strict existence checks and which can safely default to zero? Handling Option, ensure!, and checked arithmetic means validate inputs with ensure!, treat option returns explicitly, and use checked arithmetic to prevent overflow/underflow.. In practical terms, prevent underflows, validate inputs, and handle missing entries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safety pattern
keyIdea.text: Validate inputs with ensure!, treat Option returns explicitly, and use checked arithmetic to prevent overflow/underflow.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Safety Patterns

Common safety idioms

  • Use ensure! to fail early on invalid inputs.
  • Use checked_add/checked_sub for numeric operations and convert None into a clear error.
  • Handle Option returns explicitly with pattern matching or unwrap_or_default only when defaulting is safe.
// safety pattern (pseudocode)
let sender_bal = Self::balances(&sender);
ensure!(sender_bal >= amount, Error::InsufficientBalance);
let new_sender = sender_bal.checked_sub(&amount).ok_or(Error::Overflow)?;
Misconception
Using unwrap in production code or assuming a value exists can cause panics or insecure behavior. Always make absence explicit.
Key Takeaway

Be explicit about missing values and use checked arithmetic for all numeric updates.

screens.title: Assessment and design questions
screens.subtitle: Apply concepts: alternatives, trade-offs, and verification

narration.text: Let's consolidate with assessment-style reasoning. Question one asks why storing a Vec of NFT IDs under an account is problematic. The reasons are state bloat, expensive updates, and inefficient single-item checks. The better answer is to store ownership per NFT with a StorageMap and rely on off-chain indexing to build lists. Question two asks for a concrete DEX example contrasting StorageMap and StorageDoubleMap. A StorageMap suits a single identifier lookup like a user's native token balance, whereas a StorageDoubleMap suits user-asset balances where you index by account and asset to find a user's balance for a specific token. For verification, run simple checks: mint an NFT and read the NftOwner map to confirm ownership; approve a spender and verify using NftApprovals::get and contains_key; transfer and confirm that approvals were removed. A common verification pitfall is assuming events guarantee state; always check storage after the transaction. Final reflective question: which of your pallet's queries are frequent enough to warrant a double-key layout rather than repeated single-key lookups? narration.text: Summarizing the essentials: first, StorageMap maps one key to one value and is perfect for per-item lookups like balances or ownership. Second, StorageDoubleMap maps two keys to one value and is ideal for relationships like owner and spender where direct pair queries are necessary. Third, safety and performance: choose sensible hashers such as blake2_128_concat, use checked_add and checked_sub to avoid arithmetic errors, validate inputs with ensure, and avoid unbounded vectors on-chain to keep state and fees manageable. narration.text: Keep this quick reference in mind as you code. First, model per-item ownership with a StorageMap from item ID to owner so ownership checks are single-key lookups. Second, use StorageDoubleMap for relationships that are naturally two-dimensional; this gives direct pair lookups and avoids iteration. Third, always handle absence and arithmetic explicitly: contains_key for existence checks, unwrap_or_default or pattern matching for optional values when appropriate, and checked_add or checked_sub for numeric updates. These small practices reduce runtime errors, prevent state bloat, and keep gas costs predictable. When in doubt, ask whether your most frequent query will be a single-key lookup or a pair lookup—choose the structure that answers that question directly.
